grammar[0].fact: Nuremberg’s *Christkindlesmarkt* is one of the oldest in Germany, and its gingerbread, *Lebkuchen*, has been made there for over six hundred years. The market opens each year with a speech by the Christkind, a young woman with a golden crown.

grammar[1].blocks[0].text: Wem gebe ich etwas? — *dem Kind*. Was gebe ich? — *den Ball*. The answers give you the cases: dem for wem?, den for was?

grammar[1].fact: A *Wunschzettel* is the list a German child writes to the Christkind and leaves on the windowsill. It disappears during the night, and in the post office of the village of Himmelpfort, volunteers answer the letters that arrive from all over the country.

reading.intro: Christmas Eve at Lena’s. The tree is lit, Maya has come with a parcel, and for once everyone is on time. In Germany, presents are opened tonight, not tomorrow. It would have been better if they weren’t.
reading.photos[0].caption: Am Markt: Der Baum ist hoch, und der Schnee ist echt.
reading.photos[1].caption: Eine alte Karte zu Weihnachten: Vier Kinder bringen einen Baum.
reading.en: Maya: Merry Christmas, Lena! This is for you. I give it to you from the heart. · Lena: Oh, a scarf! A lovely red scarf. Wait … I know this one. · Maya: Yes? It’s brand new. · Lena: Maya. I gave it to you last year. · Maya: What? No! That was given to me by … oh. Yes. But I never wore it! It really is new! · Lena: I can see that. It’s all right. I didn’t buy it for you either. · Maya: Pardon? · Lena: Max gave it to me. Two years ago. · The doorbell rings. Max comes in and gives Lena a small bag. · Max: Merry Christmas! I’m bringing you something from my mother. And Maya, this is for you. · Maya: Thanks, Max. Who gave you the red scarf, back then? · Max: My mother. Why? · Lena: And what’s in the bag from your mother? · Max: I’ll gladly show you. She knitted it herself, she says. Red again.
reading.fact: In Germany, presents are opened on the evening of 24 December, *Heiligabend*. Children are told they come from the *Christkind* in the south, the *Weihnachtsmann* in the north. Passing one on to someone else even has a word: *weiterverschenken*.

document.intro: A page from an old German book that tells you how to write letters, with examples to copy. It is printed in *Fraktur*, the old German type: the first time looks hard, and after two minutes you can read it. You only need the headings and the names.
document.fact: Until 1941 most German books were printed in *Fraktur*. You still see it today on pub signs and newspaper mastheads. The long s looks like an f: that’s why old books seem to talk about *Haus* with an odd letter in it.
